Submission received: 18 February 2021 / Revised: 3 March 2021 / Accepted: 5 March 2021 / Published: 10 March 2021 Abstract This study investigated the effect of hemp fiber pretreatments (water and sodium hydroxide) combined with silane treatment, first on the fiber properties (microscale) and then on polylactide (PLA) composite properties (macroscale). At the microscale, Fourier transform infrared, thermogravimetric analysis, and scanning electron microscopy investigations highlighted structural alterations in the fibers, with the removal of targeted components and rearrangement in the cell wall. These structural changes influenced unitary fiber properties. At the macroscale, both pretreatments increased the composites’ tensile properties, despite their negative impact on fiber performance. Additionally, silane treatment improved composite performance thanks to higher performance of the fibers themselves and improved fiber compatibility with the PLA matrix brought on by the silane couplings. PLA composites reinforced by 30 wt.% alkali and silane treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest tensile strength (62 MPa), flexural strength (113 MPa), and Young’s modulus (7.6 GPa). Overall, the paper demonstrates the applicability of locally grown, frost-retted hemp fibers for the development of bio-based composites with low density (1.13 to 1.23 g cm−3). Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction The development of structural plant fiber composite components started about 80 years ago [1] and there is considerable interest in them nowadays because of the growing environmental and ecological pressures facing industries. Characteristics and properties of biocomposites have evolved, but improvements are still needed for the effective and durable use of plant fiber reinforcement of composites. While flax has been extensively studied in this aim [1], hemp fibers also show interesting specific properties for the reinforcement of composites [2]. The rougher surface of hemp fibers compared with flax fibers could positively influence the fiber/matrix adhesion [3]. Moreover, an increase in fiber surface roughness was found to facilitate the capillary flow in fibrous porous media, which suggests a smooth composite production process [4]. Adhesion between natural fibers and thermoplastic matrices is always questioned due to the hydrophilic character of natural fibers, which induces a decrease in the interfacial contact between the natural fiber and the matrix polymer, leads to dimensional changes and lower mechanical performance from possible moisture uptake in the composite and provides favorable conditions for the development of microorganisms. In the literature, various treatments have been investigated to improve adhesion between natural fibers and matrices, either by cleaning impurities from the surface of the fibers or by creating chemical bonding between the two components with coupling agent agents [5]. Bourmaud et al. [6] used a soft water treatment to clean flax fibers. Alkali treatments are used to remove hemicelluloses from natural fibers and can also partially remove other non-cellulosic components like lignin and pectin [7]. The removal of hemicellulose and lignin cover materials exposes more cellulose hydroxyl groups to alkali, which reduces the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers by replacing cellulose hydroxyl groups with less hydrophilic O−Na+ groups (Fiber-H + NaOH-> Fiber-O− Na+ + H2O) and improves adhesion between fibers and matrix binders [5]. Silane coupling agents are used to improve the wettability of fibers by matrix polymers through graft copolymerization. Stable covalent bonds are eventually formed between alkoxy silanes and hydroxyl groups on the fiber surface [5,8]. Fiber treatments are often conducted to improve matrix adhesion within a composite, but they may degrade the fibers’ mechanical performance at the same time [9]. As highlighted by Liu et al. [5], the effect of treatment on the mechanical properties of the fibers and resulting composites should be understood to provide effective and profitable treatments. Moreover, Merotte et al. [3] showed that the improvement of interfacial shear strength brought on by a coupling agent (MAPP vs. PP) had much less influence on the mechanical properties of the composite than the nature of the fibers (flax or hemp) and their individualization. With low interfacial shear strength systems, such as plant fibers associated with polyolefin matrices like polypropylene, polyethylene, or polylactic acid (PLA), macroscale mechanical properties are governed by the fibers’ mechanical properties and bonding area rather than by interfacial bond strength [3]. A composite’s properties depend on multiple fiber parameters (mechanical performance, content, aspect ratio, orientation, individualization and dispersion [10], adhesion with matrix [11], and porosities), so it is difficult to unquestionably attribute an improvement or diminution of the composite mechanical properties to fiber treatment. Main fiber pretreatment methods and their impact on composite performance

The most commonly used pretreatments in PLA biocomposites are alkali treatment, silane coupling agents, and physical treatments such as steam explosion and plasma treatment. These methods are favored because they either remove hydrophilic surface components or improve wettability and adhesion between the fiber and matrix, which is critical in natural fiber composites where poor interfacial compatibility often limits mechanical performance [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The review evidence explicitly identifies alkali treatment, silane coupling, and physical pretreatments as central strategies for plant fiber-reinforced PLA biocomposites [N1-R3].

Alkali treatment is especially common because it can remove hemicelluloses and other non-cellulosic components from the fiber surface, exposing more cellulose hydroxyl groups and reducing the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers. The cited Hemp/PLA study explains that alkali treatment replaces cellulose hydroxyl groups with less hydrophilic O−Na+ groups, which improves adhesion between fibers and matrix binders [N4-F2]. Silane coupling agents are also widely used because they improve wettability and form stable covalent bonds between the fiber surface and the polymer matrix. The same Hemp/PLA study notes that silane treatment improved composite performance through both higher fiber performance and improved compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The review also summarizes the effective silane structures from the silane family, indicating that coupling agents are a well-established class of pretreatment [N1-R2].

Physical pretreatments such as steam explosion and plasma treatment are also important because they can modify surface morphology and increase surface area without introducing chemical agents. The review explicitly lists these as physical pretreatment examples, alongside alkali treatment and silane coupling [N1-R3]. The Hemp/PLA study further suggests that pretreatments can alter fiber properties at the microscale, including structural changes, rearrangement in the cell wall, and improved fiber compatibility with the matrix [N4-F2].

Each pretreatment changes fiber surface chemistry, wettability, and adhesion in different ways. Alkali treatment reduces hydrophilicity by removing hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and exposing cellulose hydroxyl groups, while silane treatment improves wettability through graft copolymerization and covalent bonding [N4-F2]. Physical pretreatments likely improve surface roughness and wettability indirectly by altering fiber morphology [N1-R3]. The interfacial review material emphasizes that interfacial properties, including interdiffusion, chemical bonding, and interfacial adhesion conditions, strongly influence composite performance [N3-R1][N3-R2]. It also notes that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices, which is why pretreatment is needed to improve adhesion [N3-R5].

Performance outcomes associated with pretreatment are generally improvements in mechanical and thermal properties, but the Hemp/PLA study cautions that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance at the same time [N4-F2]. The most direct outcome evidence from the Hemp/PLA study is that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers led to the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. The review evidence further states that pretreatment can improve interfacial and mechanical properties of biocomposites [N1-F1], and that interfacial adhesion conditions are highly dependent on the fiber-matrix interface [N3-R4]. Overall, pretreatment is most effective when it improves both fiber surface compatibility and preserves enough fiber integrity to support composite strengthening [N4-F2][N3-R5].

Quantify how fiber content affects flexural strength and identify threshold behavior

The available evidence shows that flexural strength generally increases with fiber content, but the relationship is not always linear and can reach a saturation point. The Hemp/PLA study reports that, at the macroscale, both pretreatments increased composite properties, and the 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest flexural strength among the tested composites [N4-F2]. Another study on hemp fiber-reinforced composites found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased as fiber content rose [N4-R3]. However, the evidence also shows variation in the magnitude of the effect across fiber types and matrix formulations.

A direct quantification from the experimental investigation on PLA composites is that adding acetyl tributyl citrate reduced flexural strength by 22 % at fiber content of 20 wt % [N2-R1]. This is not a fiber-type comparison, but it does show that the relationship between fiber content and flexural strength is sensitive to the exact composition and processing conditions. The 3D woven flax fiber/PLA composite study reports better flexural and tensile properties, suggesting that fiber alignment and structure can substantially alter the response [N2-R3]. A separate study on PLA composites reinforced with flax and jute fibers is a review rather than a direct quantification, so it provides context rather than a numeric threshold [N2-R5].

The evidence does support the idea that a saturation point or maximum may be reached. The Hemp/PLA study indicates that the highest flexural strength was achieved at 30 wt % alkali/silane-treated hemp fibers, implying that increasing fiber content beyond that point may not produce further gains [N4-F2]. The hemp fiber composite study similarly found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but the text does not explicitly state whether the relationship continued to increase beyond a certain level [N4-R3]. The 3D printed PLA study notes that both tensile modulus and strength decreased with the increase in fiber content compared to pure PLA, though it also found a saturation behavior in some cases [N2-R4]. This is consistent with the broader idea that fiber content effects can be nonlinear and that saturation may occur depending on fiber type, matrix properties, and fabrication method.

Matrix properties and fiber alignment/modulus modulate the relationship in several ways. The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that macroscale mechanical properties are governed by the fibers’ mechanical properties and bonding area rather than solely by interfacial bond strength [N4-F2]. This means that even if a pretreatment improves adhesion, the overall flexural strength still depends on how much fiber reinforcement is actually contributing. The review material on interfacial adhesion also notes that composite properties depend on fiber parameters such as mechanical performance, content, aspect ratio, orientation, individualization, dispersion, and porosities [N3-R4]. Therefore, higher fiber content can increase flexural strength, but only if the fibers are well aligned, well dispersed, and compatible with the matrix. The evidence does not provide a universal threshold value, but it clearly supports a nonlinear relationship with possible saturation at higher fiber loadings [N4-F2][N4-R3][N2-R4].

Explain how fiber type and pretreatment interact to determine flexural strength

Different fiber types respond differently to the same pretreatment because their original surface chemistry, hydrophilicity, and mechanical performance vary. The Hemp/PLA study explains that hemp fibers have a rougher surface than flax fibers, which can positively influence fiber/matrix adhesion [N4-F2]. It also notes that the improvement in interfacial shear strength from a coupling agent had much less influence on composite mechanical properties than the nature of the fibers themselves and their individualization [N4-F2]. This suggests that fiber type is a major determinant of pretreatment effectiveness.

For fiber-matrix combinations, hemp/PLA appears to show strong strength gains when pretreated with alkali and silane. The Hemp/PLA study reports that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. This combination benefits from both the alkali removal of hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and the silane coupling that improves compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The study also emphasizes that the improvement in fiber/matrix adhesion is important, but fiber type and individualization have a larger effect on composite properties [N4-F2]. In contrast, the experimental investigation on PLA composites found that adding acetyl tributyl citrate reduced flexural strength by 22 % at 20 wt % fiber content [N2-R1], which indicates that the matrix formulation and additive chemistry can also strongly modulate the response, even for the same fiber.

The evidence also shows that fiber geometry and aspect ratio influence the overall flexural response. The Hemp/PLA study notes that longer fiber length can increase fiber strength, and that fiber surface roughness can facilitate capillary flow and improve adhesion [N4-F2]. The 3D woven flax fiber/PLA composite study reports better flexural and tensile properties, suggesting that fiber alignment and architecture are important [N2-R3]. The hemp fiber composite study also states that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but it does not explicitly separate the effect of fiber aspect ratio from that of content [N4-R3]. Still, the broader review context indicates that fiber parameters such as aspect ratio, orientation, and individualization are among the factors that affect composite properties [N3-R4].

Hemp/PLA with alkali/silane treatment is the clearest example of this interaction in the provided evidence [N4-F2]. Other fiber types, such as flax and jute, are relevant contextually, but the evidence here is less directly quantitative for those combinations [N2-R5]. Overall, the relationship between fiber type and pretreatment is nonlinear: some fibers benefit more from alkali treatment because of their hydrophilic nature, while others may benefit more from silane coupling because of matrix compatibility [N4-F2][N3-R5].

Assess failure mechanisms and environmental factors that may distort flexural strength interpretation

Common failure modes observed in PLA biocomposites include brittle fracture, fiber pull-out, and delamination or debonding at the fiber-matrix interface. The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices, leading to weak interfacial contact and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2]. The interfacial review material also notes that fiber-matrix adhesion conditions strongly influence properties and that failure behavior is tied to the interface [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The experimental investigation on PLA composites also reports that water absorption can weaken mechanical properties, indicating that failure is not only a matter of intrinsic fiber-matrix adhesion but also of environmental sensitivity [N2-R1]. The 3D-printed PLA study notes that failure mode can be analyzed based on printing parameters and aging conditions, suggesting that fabrication history and post-processing also affect how the material fails [N3-R5].

Moisture, porosity, and strain-rate effects can all alter mechanical behavior and distort flexural strength interpretation. Moisture absorption is explicitly linked to reduced mechanical performance in the Hemp/PLA study, which notes that moisture uptake can lead to dimensional changes and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2]. The water absorption study on 3D-printed sandwich composites investigates effects on mechanical performance, energy absorption, and failure modes, reinforcing the idea that moisture can change the response beyond the intrinsic material properties [N6-R1]. The study on moisture-induced changes in 3D-printed polymers evaluates changes in mechanical properties due to moisture absorption and heat, showing that environmental exposure can alter the results [N6-R2]. The study on sweat-aged PLA beams also evaluates flexural properties before and after aging in sweat, and analyzes failure mode based on printing parameters, indicating that aging and humidity can affect the mechanical response [N6-R3]. The humidity study provides a general framework for how water absorption proceeds in stages, which is relevant when interpreting long-term mechanical behavior [N6-R4].

Strain-rate effects are also important because they can change failure mode and strength. The uniaxial tensile study on PLA specimens performed under different strain rates and temperatures shows that strain-rate-dependent mechanical properties matter [N5-R1]. Although this is a tensile study, it supports the broader conclusion that flexural behavior can be strain-rate sensitive, especially in thermoplastic composites. The stress-strain curves of PLA samples with various porosity and 3D-printed design show that porosity and geometry affect load-bearing capability, load distribution, and failure mode [N5-R3]. This implies that flexural strength can be distorted by structural defects or manufacturing-induced porosity, which may not be fully captured by simple fiber-content or pretreatment comparisons.

When comparing reported flexural strength values, several caveats should be considered. First, the Hemp/PLA study warns that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance while improving matrix adhesion, making it difficult to unambiguously attribute improvements to pretreatment alone [N4-F2]. Second, the interfacial review notes that composite properties depend on multiple fiber parameters, including adhesion, content, aspect ratio, orientation, and porosity, so flexural strength cannot be interpreted in isolation [N3-R4]. Third, environmental factors such as moisture, aging, and humidity can change the actual mechanical response, as shown by the water absorption, sweat-aged PLA, and humidity studies [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Finally, fabrication method and post-processing conditions matter because the 3D-printed PLA study shows that printing parameters and aging can influence flexural behavior and failure mode [N5-R3]. Therefore, reported flexural strength should be interpreted with care, recognizing that it depends on fiber type, pretreatment, fiber content, matrix properties, alignment, porosity, moisture exposure, and test conditions [N4-F2][N3-R4][N6-R1][N5-R3].

# How different fiber pretreatment methods and fiber content affect the flexural strength of PLA biocomposites

The flexural strength of PLA biocomposites is determined by a combination of fiber pretreatment, fiber content, fiber type, and environmental factors. Pretreatment improves fiber-matrix adhesion by modifying surface chemistry and wettability, fiber content generally increases load transfer capacity but can reach a saturation point, fiber type determines how pretreatment is effective, and environmental exposure such as moisture and porosity can distort reported strength values. Below is a cohesive synthesis of these factors.

---

## 1. Pretreatment methods and their impact on flexural strength

The most commonly used pretreatments in PLA biocomposites are **alkali treatment**, **silane coupling agents**, and **physical treatments** such as steam explosion and plasma treatment [N1-R3][N1-F1]. These methods are favored because they address the main limitation of natural fiber composites: poor interfacial compatibility between hydrophilic fibers and hydrophobic polymer matrices [N3-R5]. The review evidence explicitly identifies alkali treatment, silane coupling, and physical pretreatments as central strategies for plant fiber-reinforced PLA biocomposites [N1-R3].

### 1.1 Alkali treatment
Alkali treatment is especially common because it removes hemicelluloses and other non-cellulosic components from the fiber surface, exposing more cellulose hydroxyl groups and reducing hydrophilicity. This improves adhesion between fibers and matrix binders [N4-F2]. The Hemp/PLA study explains that alkali treatment replaces cellulose hydroxyl groups with less hydrophilic O−Na+ groups, which enhances fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F2]. It also notes that alkali treatment can partially remove lignin and pectin, further improving compatibility [N4-F2].

### 1.2 Silane coupling agents
Silane coupling agents are widely used because they improve wettability and form stable covalent bonds between the fiber surface and the polymer matrix. The Hemp/PLA study reports that silane treatment improved composite performance through both higher fiber performance and improved compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The review evidence also summarizes the effective silane structures from the silane family, indicating that coupling agents are a well-established class of pretreatment [N1-R2].

### 1.3 Physical treatments
Physical treatments such as steam explosion and plasma treatment are also important because they can modify surface morphology and increase surface area without introducing chemical agents. The review explicitly lists these as physical pretreatment examples [N1-R3]. The Hemp/PLA study further suggests that pretreatments can alter fiber properties at the microscale, including structural changes, rearrangement in the cell wall, and improved fiber compatibility with the matrix [N4-F2].

### 1.4 How pretreatment changes surface chemistry, wettability, and adhesion
Each pretreatment changes the fiber surface in different ways. Alkali treatment reduces hydrophilicity by removing hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and exposing cellulose hydroxyl groups [N4-F2]. Silane treatment improves wettability through graft copolymerization and forms stable covalent bonds [N4-F2]. Physical pretreatments likely improve surface roughness and wettability indirectly by altering fiber morphology [N1-R3]. The interfacial review material emphasizes that interfacial properties, including interdiffusion, chemical bonding, and interfacial adhesion conditions, strongly influence composite performance [N3-R1][N3-R2]. It also notes that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices [N3-R5].

### 1.5 Performance outcomes of pretreatment
Pretreatment is generally associated with improved mechanical and thermal properties, but it is not always beneficial in isolation. The Hemp/PLA study warns that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance while improving matrix adhesion, making it difficult to unambiguously attribute improvements to pretreatment alone [N4-F2]. The most direct performance outcome in the evidence is that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers led to the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. The review evidence also states that pretreatment can improve interfacial and mechanical properties of biocomposites [N1-F1].

---

## 2. Fiber content and flexural strength

Flexural strength generally increases with fiber content, but the relationship is not always linear and can reach a saturation point. The Hemp/PLA study reports that both pretreatments increased composite properties, and the 30 wt.% alkali/silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest flexural strength among the tested composites [N4-F2]. Another study on hemp fiber-reinforced composites found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased as fiber content rose [N4-R3].

### 2.1 General trend
Across the evidence, the trend is broadly positive: more fiber content tends to mean more load transfer and higher flexural strength [N4-F2][N4-R3]. The Hemp/PLA study supports this by showing that increasing fiber content can produce higher flexural strength [N4-F2]. However, the evidence also shows variation in magnitude across fiber types and matrix formulations.

### 2.2 Evidence of saturation or maximum
A saturation point or maximum appears likely in some cases. The Hemp/PLA study indicates that the highest flexural strength was achieved at 30 wt.% alkali/silane-treated hemp fibers, implying that increasing fiber content beyond that point may not produce further gains [N4-F2]. The hemp fiber composite study similarly found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but it does not explicitly state whether the relationship continued to increase beyond a certain level [N4-R3]. The 3D printed PLA study notes that both tensile modulus and strength decreased with the increase in fiber content compared to pure PLA, though it also found a saturation behavior in some cases [N2-R4]. This supports the broader idea that fiber content effects can be nonlinear and that saturation may occur depending on fiber type, matrix properties, and fabrication method.

### 2.3 How matrix properties and fiber alignment/modulus modulate the relationship
The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that macroscale mechanical properties are governed by the fibers’ mechanical properties and bonding area rather than solely by interfacial bond strength [N4-F2]. This means that even if a pretreatment improves adhesion, the overall flexural strength still depends on how much fiber reinforcement is actually contributing. The review material on interfacial adhesion also notes that composite properties depend on fiber parameters such as mechanical performance, content, aspect ratio, orientation, individualization, dispersion, and porosities [N3-R4]. Therefore, higher fiber content can increase flexural strength, but only if the fibers are well aligned, well dispersed, and compatible with the matrix. The evidence does not provide a universal threshold value, but it clearly supports a nonlinear relationship with possible saturation at higher fiber loadings [N4-F2][N4-R3][N2-R4].

---

## 3. Fiber type and pretreatment interaction

Different fiber types respond differently to the same pretreatment because their original surface chemistry, hydrophilicity, and mechanical performance vary. The Hemp/PLA study explains that hemp fibers have a rougher surface than flax fibers, which can positively influence fiber/matrix adhesion [N4-F2]. It also notes that the improvement in interfacial shear strength from a coupling agent had much less influence on composite mechanical properties than the nature of the fibers themselves and their individualization [N4-F2]. This suggests that fiber type is a major determinant of pretreatment effectiveness.

### 3.1 Which fiber-matrix combinations show the strongest strength gains?
The clearest example in the evidence is **hemp/PLA** with **alkali and silane treatment**. The Hemp/PLA study reports that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. This combination benefits from both the alkali removal of hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and the silane coupling that improves compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The study also emphasizes that the improvement in fiber/matrix adhesion is important, but fiber type and individualization have a larger effect on composite properties [N4-F2].

### 3.2 How fiber geometry and aspect ratio influence the overall flexural response
Fiber geometry and aspect ratio are important because they affect load transfer and stress distribution. The Hemp/PLA study notes that longer fiber length can increase fiber strength, and that fiber surface roughness can facilitate capillary flow and improve adhesion [N4-F2]. The 3D woven flax fiber/PLA composite study reports better flexural and tensile properties, suggesting that fiber alignment and architecture are important [N2-R3]. The hemp fiber composite study also states that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but it does not explicitly separate the effect of fiber aspect ratio from that of content [N4-R3]. Still, the broader review context indicates that fiber parameters such as aspect ratio, orientation, and individualization are among the factors that affect composite properties [N3-R4].

### 3.3 General conclusion on fiber type and pretreatment interaction
The strongest strength gains occur in fiber-matrix combinations where pretreatment improves both fiber surface compatibility and preserves sufficient fiber integrity. Hemp/PLA with alkali/silane treatment is the clearest example of this interaction in the provided evidence [N4-F2]. Other fiber types, such as flax and jute, are relevant contextually, but the evidence here is less directly quantitative for those combinations [N2-R5]. Overall, the relationship between fiber type and pretreatment is nonlinear: some fibers benefit more from alkali treatment because of their hydrophilic nature, while others may benefit more from silane coupling because of matrix compatibility [N4-F2][N3-R5].

---

## 4. Failure mechanisms and environmental factors that distort flexural strength interpretation

Flexural strength is not a fixed property; it depends on the failure mechanism and environmental conditions. Common failure modes observed in PLA biocomposites include brittle fracture, fiber pull-out, and delamination or debonding at the fiber-matrix interface [N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2]. The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices, leading to weak interfacial contact and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2].

### 4.1 Moisture effects
Moisture is a major distortion factor. The Hemp/PLA study notes that moisture uptake can lead to dimensional changes and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2]. The water absorption study on 3D-printed sandwich composites investigates effects on mechanical performance, energy absorption, and failure modes, reinforcing the idea that moisture can change the response beyond the intrinsic material properties [N6-R1]. The study on moisture-induced changes in 3D-printed polymers evaluates changes in mechanical properties due to moisture absorption and heat, showing that environmental exposure can alter the results [N6-R2]. The study on sweat-aged PLA beams also evaluates flexural properties before and after aging in sweat, and analyzes failure mode based on printing parameters, indicating that aging and humidity can affect the mechanical response [N6-R3]. The humidity study provides a general framework for how water absorption proceeds in stages, which is relevant when interpreting long-term mechanical behavior [N6-R4].

### 4.2 Porosity effects
Porosity and structural defects can also alter flexural behavior. The stress-strain curves of PLA samples with various porosity and 3D-printed design show that porosity and geometry affect load-bearing capability, load distribution, and failure mode [N5-R3]. This implies that flexural strength can be distorted by manufacturing-induced porosity, which may not be fully captured by simple fiber-content or pretreatment comparisons.

### 4.3 Strain-rate effects
Strain-rate effects are also important because they can change failure mode and strength. The uniaxial tensile study on PLA specimens performed under different strain rates and temperatures shows that strain-rate-dependent mechanical properties matter [N5-R1]. Although this is a tensile study, it supports the broader conclusion that flexural behavior can be strain-rate sensitive, especially in thermoplastic composites.

### 4.4 Caveats for comparing reported flexural strength values
When comparing reported flexural strength values, several caveats should be considered. First, the Hemp/PLA study warns that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance while improving matrix adhesion, making it difficult to unambiguously attribute improvements to pretreatment alone [N4-F2]. Second, the interfacial review notes that composite properties depend on multiple fiber parameters, including adhesion, content, aspect ratio, orientation, and porosity, so flexural strength cannot be interpreted in isolation [N3-R4]. Third, environmental factors such as moisture, aging, and humidity can change the actual mechanical response, as shown by the water absorption, sweat-aged PLA, and humidity studies [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Finally, fabrication method and post-processing conditions matter because the 3D-printed PLA study shows that printing parameters and aging can influence flexural behavior and failure mode [N5-R3]. Therefore, reported flexural strength should be interpreted with care, recognizing that it depends on fiber type, pretreatment, fiber content, matrix properties, alignment, porosity, moisture exposure, and test conditions [N4-F2][N3-R4][N6-R1][N5-R3].

---

## 5. Integrated conclusion

The flexural strength of PLA biocomposites is best understood as a function of three interacting factors:

1. **Pretreatment** improves fiber-matrix adhesion and surface compatibility, but the best pretreatment depends on fiber type and matrix chemistry. Alkali treatment reduces hydrophilicity, silane coupling improves wettability and bonding, and physical treatments modify surface morphology [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F2][N1-R2].
2. **Fiber content** generally increases flexural strength, but the relationship is nonlinear and may reach a saturation point. Higher fiber content can improve load transfer, but only if the fibers are well aligned, dispersed, and compatible with the matrix [N4-F2][N4-R3][N2-R4].
3. **Fiber type** determines how pretreatment is effective. Hemp/PLA with alkali/silane treatment is the clearest example of strong strength gains, while other fibers such as flax and jute are relevant but less directly quantified in the evidence [N4-F2][N2-R5].
4. **Environmental and structural factors** can distort flexural strength. Moisture, porosity, and strain-rate effects alter mechanical behavior, and failure modes such as brittle fracture, fiber pull-out, and debonding must be considered [N4-F2][N3-R1][N6-R1][N5-R3].

In short, flexural strength in PLA biocomposites is maximized when pretreatment improves fiber-matrix adhesion, fiber content is optimized below a saturation point, fiber type is matched to the matrix, and environmental and fabrication effects are controlled. The strongest gains are often seen in combinations such as alkali/silane-treated hemp fibers in PLA, but the exact effect depends on the full system of fiber, matrix, pretreatment, content, and processing conditions [N4-F2][N1-R3][N3-R4][N6-R1].

Main fiber pretreatment methods and their impact on composite performance

The most commonly used pretreatments in PLA biocomposites are alkali treatment, silane coupling agents, and physical treatments such as steam explosion and plasma treatment. These methods are favored because they either remove hydrophilic surface components or improve wettability and adhesion between the fiber and matrix, which is critical in natural fiber composites where poor interfacial compatibility often limits mechanical performance [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The review evidence explicitly identifies alkali treatment, silane coupling, and physical pretreatments as central strategies for plant fiber-reinforced PLA biocomposites [N1-R3].

Alkali treatment is especially common because it can remove hemicelluloses and other non-cellulosic components from the fiber surface, exposing more cellulose hydroxyl groups and reducing the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers. The cited Hemp/PLA study explains that alkali treatment replaces cellulose hydroxyl groups with less hydrophilic O−Na+ groups, which improves adhesion between fibers and matrix binders [N4-F2]. Silane coupling agents are also widely used because they improve wettability and form stable covalent bonds between the fiber surface and the polymer matrix. The same Hemp/PLA study notes that silane treatment improved composite performance through both higher fiber performance and improved compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The review also summarizes the effective silane structures from the silane family, indicating that coupling agents are a well-established class of pretreatment [N1-R2].

Physical pretreatments such as steam explosion and plasma treatment are also important because they can modify surface morphology and increase surface area without introducing chemical agents. The review explicitly lists these as physical pretreatment examples, alongside alkali treatment and silane coupling [N1-R3]. The Hemp/PLA study further suggests that pretreatments can alter fiber properties at the microscale, including structural changes, rearrangement in the cell wall, and improved fiber compatibility with the matrix [N4-F2].

Each pretreatment changes fiber surface chemistry, wettability, and adhesion in different ways. Alkali treatment reduces hydrophilicity by removing hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and exposing cellulose hydroxyl groups, while silane treatment improves wettability through graft copolymerization and covalent bonding [N4-F2]. Physical pretreatments likely improve surface roughness and wettability indirectly by altering fiber morphology [N1-R3]. The interfacial review material emphasizes that interfacial properties, including interdiffusion, chemical bonding, and interfacial adhesion conditions, strongly influence composite performance [N3-R1][N3-R2]. It also notes that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices, which is why pretreatment is needed to improve adhesion [N3-R5].

Performance outcomes associated with pretreatment are generally improvements in mechanical and thermal properties, but the Hemp/PLA study cautions that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance at the same time [N4-F2]. The most direct outcome evidence from the Hemp/PLA study is that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers led to the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. The review evidence further states that pretreatment can improve interfacial and mechanical properties of biocomposites [N1-F1], and that interfacial adhesion conditions are highly dependent on the fiber-matrix interface [N3-R4]. Overall, pretreatment is most effective when it improves both fiber surface compatibility and preserves enough fiber integrity to support composite strengthening [N4-F2][N3-R5].

Quantify how fiber content affects flexural strength and identify threshold behavior

The available evidence shows that flexural strength generally increases with fiber content, but the relationship is not always linear and can reach a saturation point. The Hemp/PLA study reports that, at the macroscale, both pretreatments increased composite properties, and the 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest flexural strength among the tested composites [N4-F2]. Another study on hemp fiber-reinforced composites found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased as fiber content rose [N4-R3]. However, the evidence also shows variation in the magnitude of the effect across fiber types and matrix formulations.

A direct quantification from the experimental investigation on PLA composites is that adding acetyl tributyl citrate reduced flexural strength by 22 % at fiber content of 20 wt % [N2-R1]. This is not a fiber-type comparison, but it does show that the relationship between fiber content and flexural strength is sensitive to the exact composition and processing conditions. The 3D woven flax fiber/PLA composite study reports better flexural and tensile properties, suggesting that fiber alignment and structure can substantially alter the response [N2-R3]. A separate study on PLA composites reinforced with flax and jute fibers is a review rather than a direct quantification, so it provides context rather than a numeric threshold [N2-R5].

The evidence does support the idea that a saturation point or maximum may be reached. The Hemp/PLA study indicates that the highest flexural strength was achieved at 30 wt % alkali/silane-treated hemp fibers, implying that increasing fiber content beyond that point may not produce further gains [N4-F2]. The hemp fiber composite study similarly found that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but the text does not explicitly state whether the relationship continued to increase beyond a certain level [N4-R3]. The 3D printed PLA study notes that both tensile modulus and strength decreased with the increase in fiber content compared to pure PLA, though it also found a saturation behavior in some cases [N2-R4]. This is consistent with the broader idea that fiber content effects can be nonlinear and that saturation may occur depending on fiber type, matrix properties, and fabrication method.

Matrix properties and fiber alignment/modulus modulate the relationship in several ways. The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that macroscale mechanical properties are governed by the fibers’ mechanical properties and bonding area rather than solely by interfacial bond strength [N4-F2]. This means that even if a pretreatment improves adhesion, the overall flexural strength still depends on how much fiber reinforcement is actually contributing. The review material on interfacial adhesion also notes that composite properties depend on fiber parameters such as mechanical performance, content, aspect ratio, orientation, individualization, dispersion, and porosities [N3-R4]. Therefore, higher fiber content can increase flexural strength, but only if the fibers are well aligned, well dispersed, and compatible with the matrix. The evidence does not provide a universal threshold value, but it clearly supports a nonlinear relationship with possible saturation at higher fiber loadings [N4-F2][N4-R3][N2-R4].

Explain how fiber type and pretreatment interact to determine flexural strength

Different fiber types respond differently to the same pretreatment because their original surface chemistry, hydrophilicity, and mechanical performance vary. The Hemp/PLA study explains that hemp fibers have a rougher surface than flax fibers, which can positively influence fiber/matrix adhesion [N4-F2]. It also notes that the improvement in interfacial shear strength from a coupling agent had much less influence on composite mechanical properties than the nature of the fibers themselves and their individualization [N4-F2]. This suggests that fiber type is a major determinant of pretreatment effectiveness.

For fiber-matrix combinations, hemp/PLA appears to show strong strength gains when pretreated with alkali and silane. The Hemp/PLA study reports that 30 wt.% alkali and silane-treated hemp fibers exhibited the highest tensile strength, flexural strength, and Young’s modulus [N4-F2]. This combination benefits from both the alkali removal of hemicellulose/lignin cover layers and the silane coupling that improves compatibility with PLA [N4-F2]. The study also emphasizes that the improvement in fiber/matrix adhesion is important, but fiber type and individualization have a larger effect on composite properties [N4-F2]. In contrast, the experimental investigation on PLA composites found that adding acetyl tributyl citrate reduced flexural strength by 22 % at 20 wt % fiber content [N2-R1], which indicates that the matrix formulation and additive chemistry can also strongly modulate the response, even for the same fiber.

The evidence also shows that fiber geometry and aspect ratio influence the overall flexural response. The Hemp/PLA study notes that longer fiber length can increase fiber strength, and that fiber surface roughness can facilitate capillary flow and improve adhesion [N4-F2]. The 3D woven flax fiber/PLA composite study reports better flexural and tensile properties, suggesting that fiber alignment and architecture are important [N2-R3]. The hemp fiber composite study also states that flexural stress at break and flexural modulus increased with fiber content, but it does not explicitly separate the effect of fiber aspect ratio from that of content [N4-R3]. Still, the broader review context indicates that fiber parameters such as aspect ratio, orientation, and individualization are among the factors that affect composite properties [N3-R4].

Taken together, the strongest strength gains occur in fiber-matrix combinations where pretreatment improves both fiber surface compatibility and preserves sufficient fiber integrity. Hemp/PLA with alkali/silane treatment is the clearest example of this interaction in the provided evidence [N4-F2]. Other fiber types, such as flax and jute, are relevant contextually, but the evidence here is less directly quantitative for those combinations [N2-R5]. Overall, the relationship between fiber type and pretreatment is nonlinear: some fibers benefit more from alkali treatment because of their hydrophilic nature, while others may benefit more from silane coupling because of matrix compatibility [N4-F2][N3-R5].

Assess failure mechanisms and environmental factors that may distort flexural strength interpretation

Common failure modes observed in PLA biocomposites include brittle fracture, fiber pull-out, and delamination or debonding at the fiber-matrix interface. The Hemp/PLA study explicitly states that poor interfacial strength arises from the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers and the hydrophobic nature of polymer matrices, leading to weak interfacial contact and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2]. The interfacial review material also notes that fiber-matrix adhesion conditions strongly influence properties and that failure behavior is tied to the interface [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The experimental investigation on PLA composites also reports that water absorption can weaken mechanical properties, indicating that failure is not only a matter of intrinsic fiber-matrix adhesion but also of environmental sensitivity [N2-R1]. The 3D-printed PLA study notes that failure mode can be analyzed based on printing parameters and aging conditions, suggesting that fabrication history and post-processing also affect how the material fails [N3-R5].

Moisture, porosity, and strain-rate effects can all alter mechanical behavior and distort flexural strength interpretation. Moisture absorption is explicitly linked to reduced mechanical performance in the Hemp/PLA study, which notes that moisture uptake can lead to dimensional changes and lower mechanical performance [N4-F2]. The water absorption study on 3D-printed sandwich composites investigates effects on mechanical performance, energy absorption, and failure modes, reinforcing the idea that moisture can change the response beyond the intrinsic material properties [N6-R1]. The study on moisture-induced changes in 3D-printed polymers evaluates changes in mechanical properties due to moisture absorption and heat, showing that environmental exposure can alter the results [N6-R2]. The study on sweat-aged PLA beams also evaluates flexural properties before and after aging in sweat, and analyzes failure mode based on printing parameters, indicating that aging and humidity can affect the mechanical response [N6-R3]. The humidity study provides a general framework for how water absorption proceeds in stages, which is relevant when interpreting long-term mechanical behavior [N6-R4].

Strain-rate effects are also important because they can change failure mode and strength. The uniaxial tensile study on PLA specimens performed under different strain rates and temperatures shows that strain-rate-dependent mechanical properties matter [N5-R1]. Although this is a tensile study, it supports the broader conclusion that flexural behavior can be strain-rate sensitive, especially in thermoplastic composites. The stress-strain curves of PLA samples with various porosity and 3D-printed design show that porosity and geometry affect load-bearing capability, load distribution, and failure mode [N5-R3]. This implies that flexural strength can be distorted by structural defects or manufacturing-induced porosity, which may not be fully captured by simple fiber-content or pretreatment comparisons.

When comparing reported flexural strength values, several caveats should be considered. First, the Hemp/PLA study warns that fiber treatments may degrade fiber mechanical performance while improving matrix adhesion, making it difficult to unambiguously attribute improvements to pretreatment alone [N4-F2]. Second, the interfacial review notes that composite properties depend on multiple fiber parameters, including adhesion, content, aspect ratio, orientation, and porosity, so flexural strength cannot be interpreted in isolation [N3-R4]. Third, environmental factors such as moisture, aging, and humidity can change the actual mechanical response, as shown by the water absorption, sweat-aged PLA, and humidity studies [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Finally, fabrication method and post-processing conditions matter because the 3D-printed PLA study shows that printing parameters and aging can influence flexural behavior and failure mode [N5-R3]. Therefore, reported flexural strength should be interpreted with care, recognizing that it depends on fiber type, pretreatment, fiber content, matrix properties, alignment, porosity, moisture exposure, and test conditions [N4-F2][N3-R4][N6-R1][N5-R3].
